title: Design a OneDrive-like file sync service
brief: Users install a sync client on several devices (Windows, Mac, mobile) and expect a folder to stay in sync with the cloud and with each other. Design the backend and sync protocol, including large files, offline edits and conflicts.
constraints: 500M users, average 3 devices each
Files from bytes to 50 GB; most under 1 MB
Changes visible on other online devices within ~10 s
Offline edits must sync on reconnect without data loss
Storage efficiency matters: dedupe identical blocks

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Scope what syncs, which consistency users see and how conflicts surface.
keyPoints: Sync files and folders, renames, moves, deletes across devices
Durability: no acknowledged write is lost
Conflicts never silently drop data: keep both copies
Selective sync and files-on-demand placeholders
Sharing and versioning history (limited window)
Non-goals: real-time co-authoring of documents

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define the client-facing API for uploads, downloads and change discovery.
keyPoints: POST /uploadSession -> sessionId; PUT chunk ranges, resumable
Commit: POST /items/{id}/commit with block list and baseVersion (eTag)
GET /delta?cursor= returns changes since cursor plus new cursor
Long-poll or push (WebSocket/notification) to signal new changes
Conditional requests with If-Match eTag to detect conflicts

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model files, versions, blocks and the change journal.
keyPoints: Item(itemId, parentId, name, ownerId, currentVersion, eTag, deleted)
Version(itemId, version, blockList[], size, hash, modifiedBy)
Content-addressed blocks keyed by hash (e.g. 4 MB chunks) in blob storage with refcounts
Per-user/drive change journal ordered by sequence number; cursor = position
Metadata partitioned by driveId so one drive is one shard

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Lay out clients, metadata service, block store and notifications.
keyPoints: Client: local watcher, local DB of synced state, chunker and hasher
Front door / API gateway with auth (OAuth tokens)
Metadata service on a partitioned transactional store
Block store on blob storage, uploads directly via SAS-style signed URLs
Notification service fans out "drive changed" pings; clients then call delta
Async workers: virus scan, thumbnails, indexing, garbage collection

sections.title: Scaling
sections.prompt: Explain how this scales to hundreds of millions of drives.
keyPoints: Shard metadata by driveId; hot shared folders get special handling
Block dedupe and delta sync: only upload changed chunks
CDN / edge caching for downloads of popular shared files
Notification fan-out via pub/sub; coalesce bursts of changes
Backpressure on clients: server-driven retry-after on throttling

sections.title: Failure handling
sections.prompt: Cover interrupted uploads, conflicts, regional outages and corruption.
keyPoints: Resumable uploads; commit is atomic: version visible only after all blocks stored
Conflict on stale eTag: keep both, rename one as "name-DEVICE" copy
Geo-replicated blob storage; metadata replicated to paired region
Client-side hash verification on download; server scrubbing for bit rot
Idempotent commits with client request IDs to survive retries

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.prompt: Discuss the big design choices and their costs.
keyPoints: Block size: small improves dedupe/delta, large reduces metadata overhead
Push notifications vs polling: freshness vs connection cost
Last-writer-wins vs keep-both conflicts: simplicity vs data safety
Strong per-drive consistency vs cross-region latency
Client complexity (local state DB) vs server-driven sync

modelSummary: Split file content into content-addressed blocks in blob storage and keep metadata (items, versions, block lists) in a store partitioned by drive. Clients upload changed blocks through resumable sessions, then atomically commit a new version guarded by an eTag; a stale eTag means a conflict, resolved by keeping both copies. Other devices learn of changes through a lightweight push ping followed by a cursor-based delta call against an ordered change journal. Geo-replication, idempotent commits and hash verification protect durability.

title: Design a Teams-like presence service
brief: Show whether each user is Available, Busy, In a meeting, Away or Offline, across all their devices, and push changes to everyone who is looking at them (contact lists, chat headers, meeting rosters).
constraints: 300M monthly users, ~50M concurrently online
A user may be signed in on several devices
Presence changes propagated to watchers within ~2 s
Calendar-driven states (In a meeting) and manual overrides
Read-heavy: each user is watched by tens to hundreds of others

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define states, aggregation rules and freshness expectations.
keyPoints: States: Available, Busy, InACall, InAMeeting, DoNotDisturb, Away, Offline
Aggregate per-device presence into one user presence by priority
Manual status overrides with expiry; calendar-derived states
Away after inactivity timeout; Offline when all devices disconnect
Privacy: tenant boundaries and federation rules

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Specify publish, query and subscribe APIs.
keyPoints: PUT /presence/me {deviceId, activity, availability} as heartbeat
GET /presence?users=a,b,c batch fetch
Subscribe(userIds[]) over persistent connection; server pushes deltas
Subscriptions with TTL renewed by clients
Rate limits on subscription size per client

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Store device presence, aggregated presence and subscriptions.
keyPoints: DevicePresence(userId, deviceId, state, lastSeen) with TTL
UserPresence(userId, aggregatedState, version) computed on change
Subscriptions: watched userId -> set of connection/gateway ids
Mostly in-memory (distributed cache), not durable DB
Calendar state fed asynchronously from calendar service

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Describe the main components.
keyPoints: Edge gateways hold client WebSocket connections
Presence service partitioned by userId owns aggregation
Pub/sub layer routes changes from owner partition to gateways with subscribers
Gateways fan out to local connections
Calendar/call integrations publish events into presence service

sections.title: Scaling
sections.prompt: Explain how fan-out and heartbeat load scale.
keyPoints: Partition by userId via consistent hashing
Gateway-level subscription aggregation: one upstream subscription per gateway, not per client
Coalesce rapid flaps; debounce Away transitions
Heartbeats at long intervals; connection drop detection at gateway
Large meetings: lazy load presence for visible roster only

sections.title: Failure handling
sections.prompt: Handle node loss, missed heartbeats and partitions.
keyPoints: Presence is soft state: rebuild from client heartbeats after failover
Expire device entries via TTL so crashed clients go Offline
Gateways resubscribe on presence node failover
Degrade to "unknown" rather than wrong state when stale
Throttle reconnection storms with jittered backoff

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.prompt: Weigh push vs pull, accuracy vs cost.
keyPoints: Push gives freshness but costs connections and fan-out
Eventual consistency acceptable; strict accuracy not worth the cost
In-memory soft state vs durable storage
Heartbeat interval: battery/network cost vs staleness
Per-gateway aggregation adds hop but cuts fan-out massively

modelSummary: Treat presence as soft, in-memory state owned by a partition keyed on userId. Devices heartbeat their state and the owner aggregates them by priority into one user presence. Changes are published through pub/sub to the edge gateways that hold subscribers, and each gateway fans out to its local connections, so upstream subscriptions are aggregated per gateway. TTLs, debouncing and resubscription on failover keep the system cheap and self-healing, at the cost of eventual (seconds-level) accuracy.

title: Design a multi-tenant blob storage metadata service
brief: Design the metadata layer for an object store like Azure Blob Storage: accounts, containers and blobs, with list operations, strong consistency for a single blob and isolation between tenants.
constraints: Millions of storage accounts; some with billions of blobs
Strong read-after-write consistency per blob
List by prefix with pagination must be efficient
Per-account throughput limits (noisy neighbour protection)
Data replicated across availability zones; optional geo-replication

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define the namespace, operations and consistency guarantees.
keyPoints: Hierarchy: account -> container -> blob name (flat names, "/" as virtual dir)
Put, Get, Delete, Head, List(prefix, delimiter, marker)
Strong consistency for single-blob operations; conditional ops via eTag
Per-account limits on requests/s and bandwidth
Redundancy options: zone-redundant, geo-redundant

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Specify the metadata API used by front ends.
keyPoints: PutBlobMetadata(account, container, name, blockList, eTag-condition)
GetBlobMetadata -> location of data extents, size, eTag, properties
ListBlobs(account, container, prefix, marker, max) -> page + next marker
Lease/lock operations for exclusive writers
Internal: SplitPartition, MovePartition for load balancing

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model metadata rows and partitioning.
keyPoints: Row key = account|container|blobName, sorted lexicographically
Value: eTag, size, content-type, extent pointers, lastModified, snapshots
Range partitioning on the sorted key so prefix listing is a range scan
Partition map: key ranges -> partition server, held by a master
Write-ahead log plus checkpoints in replicated stream layer

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Describe the layers: front end, partition layer, stream/storage layer.
keyPoints: Stateless front ends authenticate and route by partition map
Partition servers own key ranges, serve reads/writes from memory table + log
Replicated append-only stream layer (3 replicas across zones) for durability
Partition master assigns ranges and handles splits/merges
Data extents stored separately from metadata

sections.title: Scaling
sections.prompt: Explain hot partitions, large accounts and load balancing.
keyPoints: Split hot ranges dynamically; merge cold ones
Avoid sequential name hotspots: advise hashed prefixes
Per-account throttling with 503 + retry-after
Caching partition map at front ends with invalidation on move
Listing uses continuation markers; never unbounded scans

sections.title: Failure handling
sections.prompt: Cover server crash, zone loss and partial writes.
keyPoints: Partition reassigned; new owner replays log from stream layer
Writes acknowledged only after quorum replication across zones
Geo-replication asynchronous: document RPO, failover is account-level
Idempotent writes with client request IDs
Orphaned data extents garbage collected via refcount/scan

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.prompt: Discuss key choices.
keyPoints: Range vs hash partitioning: range enables listing, hash spreads load
Strong consistency in-region vs async geo-replication (RPO > 0)
Single owner per range simplifies consistency but needs fast failover
Separating metadata and data paths: complexity vs independent scaling
Throttling protects neighbours but surfaces errors to clients

modelSummary: Use a layered architecture: stateless front ends, a partition layer that range-partitions metadata on account|container|blob so prefix listing is a range scan, and a replicated append-only stream layer that writes synchronously across availability zones. Each range has one owning partition server, which gives strong per-blob consistency; a master splits hot ranges and reassigns them on failure, and the new owner replays the log. Per-account throttling isolates tenants. Geo-replication is asynchronous, so cross-region failover has a non-zero RPO.

title: Design a distributed cache service
brief: Design a managed, Redis-like distributed cache that many internal services use to cut latency and database load. It should scale out, survive node loss and offer sensible eviction and consistency semantics.
constraints: 1M+ ops/s per large cluster, p99 < 2 ms
Datasets up to several TB in memory
Key/value with TTL; values up to 1 MB
Node failures must not cause a thundering herd on the backing DB
Multiple tenants (services) share the platform

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Clarify semantics: cache-aside vs write-through, TTL, eviction, consistency.
keyPoints: Get/Set/Delete with TTL; optional atomic increment and compare-and-set
Cache is not source of truth: loss is tolerable, staleness bounded by TTL
Eviction policy: LRU / LFU approximations
Tenant isolation: quotas on memory and ops
Non-goals: durable storage, complex queries

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define client and admin APIs.
keyPoints: get(key) / set(key, value, ttl) / delete(key) / cas(key, expected, value)
Batch mget/mset to amortise round trips
Smart client library with cluster topology and consistent hashing
Admin: create cache, scale shards, set eviction policy
Metrics endpoint for hit rate, evictions, latency

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Describe memory layout and key distribution.
keyPoints: Hash slots (e.g. 16384) mapped to shards
Per-shard hash table plus approximate LRU clock
Primary + replica per shard
Slot map versioned and gossiped / served by config service
Large values discouraged; compression optional

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Lay out clients, shards, replicas and control plane.
keyPoints: Client-side routing via slot map; MOVED redirects on topology change
Shards with async replication to replicas in another zone
Control plane monitors health, promotes replicas, rebalances slots
Optional proxy tier for simple clients
Backing DB accessed by services on miss (cache-aside)

sections.title: Scaling
sections.prompt: Scale throughput and handle hot keys.
keyPoints: Add shards and migrate slots online
Hot keys: client-side near cache, key replication, or read from replicas
Connection pooling and pipelining
Request coalescing (single-flight) to stop stampedes on miss
Jittered TTLs to avoid synchronized expiry

sections.title: Failure handling
sections.prompt: Handle node failure, split brain and cold starts.
keyPoints: Replica promotion on primary failure; some recent writes may be lost
Fencing via epoch numbers to avoid two primaries
Warm-up: gradual traffic shift, prefetch hot keys
Clients fall back to DB with circuit breaker and rate limit
Invalidate on write in source of truth to bound staleness

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.prompt: Discuss trade-offs.
keyPoints: Async replication: low latency vs possible lost writes on failover
Client-side vs proxy routing: latency vs simplicity
LRU vs LFU: recency vs frequency workloads
Cache-aside vs write-through: simplicity vs freshness
Strong consistency is expensive; cache usually accepts staleness

modelSummary: Shard keys into hash slots that map to primary/replica shard pairs, and have smart clients route requests with a versioned slot map. Replication to replicas in other zones is asynchronous, so failover is fast but may lose the last few writes; epochs fence off stale primaries. Hot keys are handled with near caches and replica reads, stampedes with single-flight loading and jittered TTLs, and tenants with quotas. The cache is never the source of truth, which is what makes those relaxed guarantees acceptable.

title: Design a telemetry ingestion pipeline at scale
brief: Every service and device across a cloud platform emits logs, metrics and traces. Design the ingestion pipeline that accepts this data, makes it queryable within a minute and feeds alerting.
constraints: Tens of millions of events/s at peak, multiple PB/day
Ingest-to-query latency < 60 s; alerting on metrics < 30 s
Bursty producers; must not lose data during downstream outages
Schemas evolve independently per team
Retention tiers: hot 7-30 days, cold archive for longer

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Scope signal types, latency, durability and query needs.
keyPoints: Logs, metrics (time series) and distributed traces
At-least-once delivery; dedupe where it matters
Hot query store for recent data; cheap cold archive
Alerting on metrics with low latency
Multi-tenant: per-team quotas, access control, PII handling

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Define the ingestion and query interfaces.
keyPoints: Batch HTTP/gRPC ingest endpoint with compression; OpenTelemetry-style schema
Local agent buffers and batches on each host
Response codes for throttling with retry-after
Query API with time range, filters, aggregations
Alert rule API: query + threshold + window

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model events, metrics and storage layout.
keyPoints: Event: tenant, source, timestamp, schemaVersion, attributes, body
Metrics pre-aggregated into time buckets keyed by (metric, dimensions)
Columnar storage partitioned by tenant and time
Trace spans keyed by traceId for lookup
Schema registry for versions and field types

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Draw the pipeline end to end.
keyPoints: Host agent -> regional ingestion front ends
Durable partitioned log (Event Hubs/Kafka-like) as buffer
Stream processors: parse, enrich, scrub PII, route by type
Sinks: columnar log store, time-series DB, trace store, cold blob archive
Alerting evaluates on stream or time-series DB

sections.title: Scaling
sections.prompt: Explain scaling under bursts and growth.
keyPoints: Partition the log by tenant+source; add partitions as volume grows
Agent-side batching, compression and sampling (traces, debug logs)
Autoscale stream processors on lag
Per-tenant quotas to stop one team flooding the pipeline
Downsample/rollup old metrics; tier to cheap storage

sections.title: Failure handling
sections.prompt: Handle outages and bad data.
keyPoints: Durable log absorbs sink outages; replay from offsets
Agents spill to local disk when ingestion unavailable
Dead-letter queue for unparseable events
Monitor the monitor: independent health path for pipeline itself
Regional isolation so one region failure does not affect others

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.prompt: Discuss key trade-offs.
keyPoints: Sampling cuts cost but loses rare events
At-least-once plus idempotent sinks vs exactly-once complexity
Schema-on-write (fast queries) vs schema-on-read (flexibility)
Pre-aggregation reduces cost but fixes dimensions
Regional pipelines vs global view: cross-region queries fan out

modelSummary: Host agents batch, compress and spill to disk, and send to regional ingestion front ends that write to a durable partitioned log. That log decouples bursty producers from consumers. Stream processors parse, enrich and scrub the data and route it to specialised sinks: a columnar store for logs, a time-series database for metrics, a trace store and a cold blob archive. Alerting evaluates metrics in near real time. Quotas, sampling, rollups and replay from log offsets keep the pipeline affordable and resilient.

title: Design a global configuration and feature rollout service with safe deployment rings
brief: Thousands of services need dynamic configuration and feature flags. Changes must roll out progressively (rings: internal, canary region, broad regions) with health gates and fast rollback, because a bad config can take down a global service.
constraints: 50k services/instances groups, ~5M running processes reading config
Config reads must never be on the critical path to a remote call
Rollout across 60+ regions over hours to days, rollback in minutes
Full audit trail and approvals for production changes
Config service outage must not break running services

sections.title: Requirements & scope
sections.prompt: Define what is configured, who changes it and the safety guarantees.
keyPoints: Typed key/values and feature flags with targeting (region, tenant, % of users)
Progressive rollout through rings with bake time and health gates
Instant global kill switch for emergencies
Audit, approval and validation (schema, policy checks) before rollout
Clients keep working on last known good config

sections.title: API
sections.prompt: Specify authoring, rollout and client APIs.
keyPoints: Author: PUT /configs/{ns}/{key} creates new immutable version
Rollout: POST /rollouts {version, ringPlan, gates}; pause/resume/rollback
Client SDK: get(key) from local snapshot; onChange callbacks
Watch/stream endpoint or periodic poll with version eTag
Evaluation context for flags: tenant, region, user hash

sections.title: Data model
sections.prompt: Model versions, rings and rollout state.
keyPoints: ConfigVersion(namespace, version, content, author, approvals, hash)
Ring definitions: ordered sets of regions/scale units
Rollout(id, version, currentRing, state, gateResults, startedAt)
Per-target desired version vs observed version
Immutable history enables rollback by pointer flip

sections.title: High-level architecture
sections.prompt: Describe control plane and data plane.
keyPoints: Control plane: authoring, validation, approvals, rollout orchestrator
Orchestrator advances rings after bake time and healthy signals
Data plane: regional config caches/CDN serving signed snapshots
Client SDK caches snapshot in memory and on disk
Health signals from telemetry pipeline feed gates

sections.title: Scaling
sections.prompt: Explain how it scales to millions of readers.
keyPoints: Clients read locally; only fetch on version change
Regional read replicas and CDN distribute snapshots
Delta or compressed snapshots per namespace
Jittered polling / push notification to avoid thundering herd
Namespacing limits blast radius and payload size

sections.title: Failure handling
sections.prompt: Handle bad configs, outages and partial rollouts.
keyPoints: Automatic rollback when health gates fail (error rate, latency, crashes)
Last-known-good on disk if config service unreachable at startup
Signed snapshots so clients reject corrupt/tampered content
Validation and canary prevent malformed config reaching broad rings
Stuck rollouts alert owners; pausing is always safe

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.prompt: Discuss trade-offs.
keyPoints: Speed of rollout vs safety (bake time per ring)
Push vs poll: propagation latency vs load and complexity
Central control plane vs regional autonomy
Emergency bypass of rings is needed but must be audited and rare
Flag debt: flags need lifecycle and cleanup

modelSummary: Separate a control plane (authoring, validation, approvals and a rollout orchestrator) from a highly available data plane that serves signed, immutable config snapshots through regional caches. Client SDKs read from an in-memory snapshot that is also saved on disk, so a config service outage never breaks running services. The orchestrator moves each version through rings, from internal to canary region to broader waves, with bake times and health gates fed by telemetry, and rolls back automatically by pointing targets at the previous immutable version. An audited kill switch covers emergencies.
